content.description: Hello HN! I want to share something me and a few friends have been working on for a while now — Zeroshot, a web tool that builds image classifiers using text-image models and autolabeling. What does this mean in practice? You can put together an image classifier in about 30 seconds that’s faster and more accurate than CLIP, but that you can deploy yourself however you’d like. It’s open source, commercially licensed, and doesn’t require you to pay anyone per API call. Here's a 2 minute video that shows it off: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S4R1gtmM-Lo How/why does it work? We believe that with the rise of foundation vision models, computer vision will fundamentally change. These powerful models will let any devs “compile” a model ahead of time with a subset of the foundation model’s characteristics, using only text and a web-tool. The days of teams of MLEs building complex models and pipelines are ending. Zeroshot works by using two powerful pre-trained models, CLIP and DINOv2 together. The web-app allows users to quickly create our training sets via text search. Using pre-cached DINOv2 features, we generate a simple linear model that can be trained and deployed without any fine-tuning. Since you can see what’s going into your training set, you can tune your prompts to get the type of performance or detail you want. CLIP Small -- Size: 335 MB, Latency: 35ms CLIP Large -- Size: 891 MB, Latency: 276ms Zeroshot -- Size: 85 MB, Latency: 20ms What’s next? We wanna see how people use or would use the tool before deciding what to do next. On the list: clients for iOS and NodeJS, speeding up GPU inference times via TensorRT, offering larger Zeroshot models for better accuracy, easier results refining, support for bringing your own data lake, model refinement using GPT-V, we’ve got plenty of ideas.

The broker solves three major challenges that are especially relevant in corporate environments: (A) Enable users to delegate workloads to agents without providing the agents all the user’s tokens. (B) Connect fragmented identity and authorization systems. (C) Centralize tool approvals and audit logging. We built AIB to fill an infrastructure gap in our own agent platform. At this moment in time, IETF working groups are still finalizing standards for agent identity, and vendors are still turning the necessary infrastructure into off-the-shelf products. We needed that infrastructure today. How it works: the user consents once per agent and service. The broker stores the third-party tokens encrypted. At request time a gateway (e.g. Agentgateway) does RFC 8693 token exchange. Agents never see user tokens and MCP servers only implement tools and don’t need to care about all the OAuth 2.1 plumbing. AIB is v0.1 and runs in production, bringing together hundreds of our agents with dozens of internal and external MCP servers. To try it locally: clone the repo, run "just compose-up-detached". The current features focus on on-behalf-of (OBO) use cases, where human actors delegate to agents. Next we are looking to also support headless agents, where agents are invoked by machines. Intent-based authorization is yet another package on our roadmap. If you’ve built either, or have feedback on the UI/UX, I’d like to hear from you!

content.description: Hi HN, I built cc-pair because I kept noticing that when a coding agent reviews its own work, it tends to go easy on it. cc-pair pairs the two agents I already use — Claude Code and Codex — so one authors a change and the other reviews it, and they iterate until the reviewer approves or the round limit (default 3) escalates to the human. Roles are symmetric: either agent can be author or reviewer. In auto mode, `pair start --as claude` (or `--as codex`) opens the author and starts the other agent as reviewer for each round — no second terminal needed. In manual mode you run both yourself. They communicate through numbered message files in a shared directory (~/.pair/<repo>-<hash>/), so the whole review thread is inspectable on disk. Install: npm install -g claude-codex-pair (Node 22+, macOS/Linux for auto mode; manual mode works on Windows). Both CLIs need to be installed and signed in. Repo: https://github.com/leonlee/cc-pair — the README has an example review thread in Appendix A, and DESIGN.md specifies the protocol. I'd love feedback: does cross-model review actually catch things self-review misses in your experience, and what would you want the reviewer to be stricter about?

content.description: Hi folks, Alex here from ThunderPhone. Today we're launching v2. Voice AI has been a hot topic for the past year or two, both for automating phone calls and for adding voice features to apps. Most of the voice agents deployed have been using a "3 step pipeline": a transcription model to turn user speech into text, an LLM to generate a response in text, and a TTS model to turn the response text into audio. But the performance of these 3-step voice agents has often been so-so, largely for 3 reasons: 1) Voice agents have to be fast, usually requiring non-thinking LLMs to handle the conversation. Non-thinking LLMs make mistakes, leading to dumb behavior that derails conversations. 2) Today's voice AI stacks typically rely on a single transcription model to turn what the user says into text. This step loses a ton of information from the audio, and if the transcription model makes a mistake, the LLM often has no way to recover. This also leads to a lot of dumb behavior that breaks calls. 3) Natural conversation handling is a hard problem - filtering out noise like background voices, knowing when to allow the AI to be interrupted by a "uh, wait" but not by an "uh-huh", etc. - this also leads to awkward conversations. The "bitter lesson-pilled" solution to all of these is most likely going to be a "full duplex" model that receives and emits audio at all times, allowing for fluid back-and-forth, while also calling a smarter model behind the scenes. OpenAI appears to have been the first to make real progress towards this architecture with their latest GPT-Live release, but that tech is not yet ready to plug into phone calls. In the meantime, we've stitched together a stack that improves the performance of phone calls far beyond what's possible with a 3-step pipeline. The ThunderPhone stack combines a few insights: 1) Grabbing signal from audio in more than one way, including running multiple transcription models at once, and piping audio directly into LLMs. This hugely reduc…

You hold down Control-Option-Space, speak or type your task, be it complex or a simple browser search, and Atticus will get on it. The interesting part is that simple tasks, like opening apps, playing a Spotify playlist, or web queries, don't touch AI, and instead are processed locally and typically finish in under a second. For example, prompting Atticus to open apps takes around 0.08 seconds, sometimes even finishing before you finish your sentence, sort of like Jev. Any tasks that are more complicated will be sent to Claude via claude -p, meaning you never need an API key and Atticus will run on your existing Claude Pro or Max plan. By using this approach, costs are also cut down immensely, with, on average, tasks costing a fraction of a cent. To achieve Atticus' speed, it remembers shortcuts from each task it completes. When it does a task right for the first time, it saves its steps and replays them the next time without AI. For example, a workflow of creating a new meeting took about 30 seconds the first time around. Atticus then logs the exact steps to memory and takes 5-8 seconds on the next pass. To add to this, Atticus also learns about you as you use it more and from what's on your computer, including your name, your apps, and things you want it to remember, personalizing its answers to you. To combat the safety concerns over giving an AI unrestricted access to your device, Atticus has toggleable restrictions, so before anything is deleted, sent, bought, or written to a file, the user is prompted before that action. Some features I'm currently working on include a meeting copilot that capitalizes on Atticus' speed, allowing Atticus to listen in on meetings and answer questions in real time as they come in, personalized to the context of the meeting and what it knows about you. content.description: Like any side project, Remarc started with my own problem: there was no good way to give AI coding agents contextual feedback on their own output. There are plenty of tools for collaborating with humans, but surprisingly few for collaborating with AI. Chat was not cutting it for the feedback I wanted to give: This thing in the implementation plan? Change it to that. What did you mean here? See this button? Here is a screenshot. I circled it because it is missing a hover state. This sentence in the third paragraph? Rephrase it. If you are an opinionated builder, this gets clunky quickly. You either dictate paragraphs of messy feedback or resolve every detail one by one. AI is good at parsing mess, but garbage in, garbage out still applies. I could get products to 90% quickly. The last 10% of feedback and polish was the bottleneck. So I built Remarc. Remarc lets you select text in any Mac app, capture and annotate a screenshot, or comment on a web element. Each comment keeps its original context, status, and session. A connected agent can read the session, work through it, update statuses, and leave resolution summaries over MCP. Think of it like leaving comments on a google doc vs sending a long rambling feedback note via Slack - the more granular you get with your feedback, the more it benefits from structure & better context. Remarc is free and open source, with no account, subscription, or telemetry. https://remarc.app/ https://github.com/metedata/Remarc

content.description: I run long sessions with Claude. For a long time I've had Claude in the middle of some difficult coding task, and then I see the auto-compact message pop up. Every time I wonder if Claude actually picks everything up correctly and nothing is lost. Claude told me 78/82 auto-compactions landed while Claude was working. For a while I couldn't do much. At first I made a skill that would make Claude explicitly save progress throughout long runs. But that didn't fix the core problem and cost more tokens as well. Now that mods came out, I fixed the actual problem. catnap tells Claude at 50% context what the context is and that it should finish what it's working on, write a handoff, and then initialize compaction itself. When Claude finishes its task, catnap compacts, and Claude can then pick up work again. The handoff replaces Claude Code's default summary, so we don't do similar work twice. If Claude for some reason doesn't compact before 60%, it gets a stricter note. And Claude Code's default auto-compact kicks in at 70% as a backstop. The 3 numbers are all settings. After I took on catnap, 0 of 129 naps came mid-task: 98 of them in benchmarks and 31 in my own sessions. The cost is the same as the default auto-compact kicking in at the same point, in tokens and dollars, on 200K and 1M context windows. Compared to the default auto-compaction that kicks in when context is nearly full, catnap used 56% fewer tokens. But lowering the default auto-compact will get you most of the way there as well. I measured memory today as well. Claude worked through tasks one message at a time while 20 instructions and facts were said in the chat, inside long chatty messages, and nowhere else. Asked right after compaction to list them from memory, no file reads: all 20 were listed with catnap and with the default compaction, in every run (15 with catnap, 5 with the default). content.description: Stof is an open-source runtime for logic you don't own or fully trust. Imagine a JSON document with functions inside, scoped to just the document that contains them. Stof instantiates this doc as a small wasm env, and makes these functions safe to call. They can't access or manipulate anything but their own doc. WebAssembly by itself is large in binary form, requires a lot of tooling, etc. Stof can be sent over the wire easily, is a superset of JSON for compatibility, and keeps the guarantees. I created Stof not to replace a data format or anything, but to be a glue layer for data and distributed systems to work with one another. This includes I/O for interchange data like JSON, YAML, TOML, etc., but also complex data like PDFs, images, binaries, both structured and unstructured (good layer to turn one into the other). The fact is, the layer of data and communication between apps tends to be a bit messy, and strict adapters compiled at build time tend to be insufficient for the dynamism of modern software. This applies directly to AI-generated data and code, which is basically like calling into another untrusted service. With this, you can safely embed the execution, pick where things run, and combine harnesses like data. Works well as a "living" context, also with the JSON interop - just parse into or stringify sections of the Stof doc at runtime when needed, like agent tool defs. The playground on the site runs entirely in your browser. Stof is written in Rust and has support for JS/TS and Python today. I'd especially like feedback on whether the idea makes sense from the landing page, and where the docs need help. GitHub: https://github.com/dev-formata-io/stof Thank you!! -CJ

content.description: Hi, I’m Pavel. I’ve been building Relay, a self-hostable AI gateway. The main thing I wanted to solve was smart routing without turning the gateway itself into a bottleneck. Relay can classify an incoming request, decide what kind of model capabilities the request needs, then route it across your configured providers while also accounting for limits and available capacity. It ships with routing classification models I’ve trained specifically for this problem, with the option of swapping that piece for Laya or other System One models. This started when I was trying to string together several providers’ free tiers. I kept hitting rate limits at different intervals, which broke some of my agent clients. Some agents were also getting greedy with shared resources, so I needed a way to manage how they used the available capacity. That led to Relay’s queue-first approach. Sometimes it’s better to wait a second or two for your preferred model than immediately fall back to another one. Relay queues and paces requests against configured provider limits, aiming to make use of available capacity without repeatedly hitting rate-limit errors or needlessly falling back to worse models. Relay’s classification model also looks for signals that a request needs specific capabilities, such as coding or more complex reasoning, while classifying the request’s main intent before routing anything. One thing I’ve obsessed over is keeping that decision layer cheap. Relay’s built-in classifier runs in the single digit millisecond range. It has a deliberately narrow job: classifying LLM requests and helping decide where to send them. It probably won’t be playing DOOM, but that’s a trade off I’m happy with for a routing layer. In the routing tests I've run so far, the built-in classifier is considerably faster than Laya while producing broadly similar routing decisions.
